core: working definition of a supply chain: the network of organizations that moves materials and products from raw inputs to the customer
the five stages: suppliers, manufacturers, distributors, retailers, customers
why the chain matters: every link affects cost and speed
inventory: stock held to meet demand, and the too-much/too-little trade-off
supply chain risk: disruptions ripple through the chain
supporting: production as the conversion of inputs into outputs
outOfScope: operations management in depth (own topic: operations)
global trade and international business (own topic: global-business)
practitioner logistics management (route optimization, warehousing systems, forecasting models)

claims.claim: A supply chain is the network of organizations that moves materials and products from raw inputs to the final customer; supply chain management coordinates the activities of all chain members into a seamless, customer-driven process whose goal is a satisfied customer.
The main stages of a supply chain are suppliers, manufacturers, distributors, retailers, and customers.
Every link in a supply chain affects the cost and speed of delivering products; in many industries, materials and supplies amount to as much as half of a company's sales revenue.

Logistics is the process that coordinates acquiring, transporting, and storing materials and inventory; it is the movement-and-storage function within the broader supply chain, concerned with getting the right item, in the right quantity, at the right time, to the right place.
Inventory is the stock of goods a company holds for use in production or for sale to customers, including raw materials, work in progress, and finished goods.

Holding too much inventory ties up money, adds storage costs, and risks obsolescence, while holding too little risks running out and disappointing customers; inventory management balances holding and ordering costs against keeping enough on hand.

Supply chains are vulnerable to disruption: a problem at one link, such as a supplier failure, a transport delay, or a disaster, can ripple through the chain and reach customers, because the chain depends on coordination among all members.

Production converts inputs such as natural resources, raw materials, human resources, and capital into outputs, which are products and services; managing that conversion process is the role of operations managers.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether logistics and supply chain management mean the same thing
positions: Some business writing uses the terms interchangeably, treating logistics as the entire flow of goods

CFI and this lesson treat logistics as the movement-and-storage function inside the broader discipline of supply chain management, which also covers sourcing, production planning, inventory decisions, and relationships
conflictingEvidence.resolution: This lesson adopts the narrower, function-based distinction: logistics moves and stores goods; supply chain management coordinates the entire network.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the customer counts as a stage of the supply chain
positions: Some textbook treatments list only suppliers, manufacturers, wholesalers, and retailers as chain members
This lesson includes customers as the final link because OpenStax frames the chain as customer driven and existing to serve customers
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson keeps customers as the fifth stage, consistent with OpenStax's customer-driven framing of supply chain management.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Business, 12.4 Using Supply Chain Management to Increase Efficiency and Customer Satisfaction
sourceRecords.notes: Verified live via HTTP on 2026-08-21 (section 12.4; the registry's existing production-operations record references this section, but this is a new id for the 12.4 page itself). Supports: the goal of supply-chain management (creating a satisfied customer by coordinating all supply-chain members' activities into a seamless process), customer-driven chains, chain members (suppliers, manufacturers, wholesalers, retailers), supply-chain manager responsibilities (sourcing and procurement, scheduling production, managing inventory, transport and storage, order processing, coordinating customer service and information flows), and the stakes of late delivery. Concepts adapted into original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Business, 10.4 Pulling It Together: Resource Planning
sourceRecords.notes: Verified live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Supports: inventory as the supply of goods held for use in production or for sale to customers; the inventory trade-off (large inventories meet production and customer demand and earn quantity discounts, but tie up money, cost to store, and can become obsolete); the goal of inventory management (keeping down ordering and holding costs while maintaining enough on hand for production and sales); materials and supplies amounting to as much as half of sales revenue in many industries; and the priority of building relationships with quality suppliers. Concepts adapted into original prose.
